lessons.title: What is biology?
lessons.lead: Biology is the scientific study of living things: what they are made of, how they work, how they develop, how they interact and how they came to be. This lesson maps the subject and the big ideas that tie it together.
objectives: Describe what biologists study, from molecules to the biosphere
Name the unifying ideas of biology: cells, genes, evolution, energy and homeostasis
Explain how biology connects with chemistry, physics and mathematics

lessons.title: Characteristics of living organisms
lessons.lead: Living things share a set of properties that, taken together, distinguish them from non-living matter. This lesson describes those properties and uses them to discuss borderline cases such as viruses.
objectives: List and explain the characteristics shared by living organisms
Apply the characteristics to decide whether something is alive
Explain why viruses are a borderline case

lessons.title: Levels of biological organisation
lessons.lead: Living things are organised in a hierarchy, from atoms and molecules through cells, tissues, organs and organisms to populations, communities, ecosystems and the biosphere. Each level has emergent properties that the levels below don't have.
objectives: Put the levels of biological organisation in order
Explain what an emergent property is, with examples
Relate a process at one level to its effects at another

lessons.title: The characteristics of life
lessons.lead: How do we know whether a newly discovered organism, a dormant seed or a frozen bacterium is alive? This lesson applies the characteristics of life to real cases and looks at how life is detected in practice.
objectives: Apply the characteristics of life to dormant, extreme and unusual cases
Describe practical tests used to detect life
Explain why scientists use several criteria together

lessons.title: Classification and taxonomy
lessons.lead: With an estimated several million species alive today, biologists need a system to name and organise them. Taxonomy names and classifies organisms in a hierarchy; modern classification aims to reflect evolutionary relationships.
objectives: Put the taxonomic ranks in order
Write a species name correctly using binomial nomenclature
Explain why modern classification is based on evolutionary relationships

lessons.title: The three domains of life
lessons.lead: All living organisms fall into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. The division, proposed by Carl Woese in the 1970s and 1990 from ribosomal RNA sequences, revealed that "prokaryotes" are two very different groups.
objectives: Name the three domains and give examples of each
Compare Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya
Describe the molecular evidence for the three-domain system

lessons.title: The kingdoms of life
lessons.lead: Within the domain Eukarya, organisms are traditionally divided into kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi and protists. Older schemes included kingdoms for prokaryotes too. This lesson compares the kingdoms and explains why "protists" are not a natural group.
objectives: Describe the main features of animals, plants, fungi and protists
Classify an unfamiliar eukaryote into a kingdom from its features
Explain why protists don't form a monophyletic group

lessons.title: Scientific method
lessons.lead: Science is a way of finding out about the natural world by testing ideas against evidence. This lesson describes the cycle of observation, hypothesis, prediction, experiment and conclusion, and what makes it reliable.
objectives: Describe the steps of the scientific method as a cycle
Distinguish a hypothesis from a theory
Explain why peer review and replication matter

lessons.title: Hypotheses and predictions
lessons.lead: A good investigation starts with a clear hypothesis and a precise prediction. This lesson shows how to write testable hypotheses, null and alternative hypotheses, and predictions that follow from them.
objectives: Write a testable hypothesis and a prediction for an investigation
Distinguish null and alternative hypotheses
Explain why a prediction must follow logically from the hypothesis

lessons.title: Variables and experimental design
lessons.lead: A fair experiment changes one factor, measures its effect on another and keeps everything else the same. This lesson defines independent, dependent and control variables and shows how to design a valid experiment.
objectives: Identify independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation
Design an experiment that tests one variable fairly
Explain the role of replicates and sample size

lessons.title: Controls and reproducibility
lessons.lead: Controls show that a result is caused by the factor being tested and not by something else. Reproducibility, getting the same result when an experiment is repeated by others, is what turns a single finding into trusted knowledge.
objectives: Distinguish positive, negative and placebo controls
Explain the difference between repeatability and reproducibility
Describe why the "reproducibility crisis" matters and how it is being addressed

lessons.title: Accuracy and precision
lessons.lead: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. A measurement can be precise but inaccurate. This lesson separates the two and links them to types of error.
objectives: Distinguish accuracy, precision and resolution
Relate random error to precision and systematic error to accuracy
Suggest how to improve the accuracy and precision of a measurement

lessons.title: Reliability and validity
lessons.lead: A result is reliable if it can be obtained consistently, and valid if it actually measures what it claims to and answers the question asked. This lesson explains both, and how evidence is judged.
objectives: Define reliability and validity and give examples of threats to each
Evaluate whether a conclusion is supported by the evidence
Explain why correlation doesn't prove causation

lessons.title: Biological measurements
lessons.lead: Biologists measure things across an enormous range of scales, from nanometre-sized molecules to whole ecosystems. This lesson covers how sizes, masses, volumes and rates are measured, and how to calculate magnification.
objectives: Choose suitable instruments and units for biological measurements
Calculate actual size from magnification and image size
Use a calibrated eyepiece graticule to measure cells

lessons.title: Units and conversions
lessons.lead: Science uses the International System of Units (SI) so that measurements can be compared worldwide. This lesson covers base units, prefixes and the conversions biologists use most.
objectives: Use SI base units and prefixes correctly
Convert between units of length, mass, volume and concentration
Express rates with appropriate units

lessons.title: Scientific notation
lessons.lead: Biology deals with numbers from the 10⁻¹⁰ m of an atom to the 10¹³ cells of a human body. Scientific notation (standard form) writes such numbers compactly and makes calculations with them easier.
objectives: Write very large and very small numbers in standard form
Multiply and divide numbers in standard form
Use significant figures appropriately

lessons.title: Graphs and data presentation
lessons.lead: Choosing the right table or graph makes patterns in data clear and honest. This lesson covers results tables, line graphs, bar charts, histograms and scatter graphs, and how to draw and read them.
objectives: Construct a results table with correct headings and units
Choose the appropriate type of graph for a data set
Describe and interpret trends, including rates from gradients

lessons.title: Statistical foundations
lessons.lead: Living things vary, so biologists need statistics to summarise data and decide whether differences are real or due to chance. This lesson covers averages, spread, the normal distribution and choosing a statistical test.
objectives: Calculate mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation
Describe the normal distribution and the meaning of standard deviation
Choose an appropriate statistical test and interpret a p-value

lessons.title: Sampling methods
lessons.lead: Biologists can rarely measure every individual, so they study samples. A sample is only useful if it represents the population fairly. This lesson covers random, systematic and stratified sampling and the methods used in ecology.
objectives: Explain why samples must be representative and large enough
Describe random, systematic and stratified sampling
Estimate population size using quadrats and mark–release–recapture

lessons.title: Ethical considerations in biological research
lessons.lead: Biological research can involve animals, human volunteers, human tissue and data, and organisms that could affect the environment. This lesson sets out the main ethical principles and how research is regulated, with UK examples.
objectives: Explain the 3Rs and how animal research is regulated in the UK
Describe the principles of research with human participants, including informed consent
Discuss ethical issues around genetic information, biodiversity and dual-use research

lessons.title: Cell theory
lessons.lead: Cell theory says that every living thing is made of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that new cells come only from existing cells. This lesson tells how the idea was built from microscope evidence and why it still matters.
objectives: State the three principles of cell theory
Describe the observations that led to it, and who made them
Calculate magnification and actual size from a microscope image

lessons.title: Prokaryotic cells
lessons.lead: Prokaryotes, the bacteria and archaea, are cells without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. They are small and structurally simple, yet they are the most abundant and metabolically varied organisms on Earth.
objectives: Describe the structures found in a prokaryotic cell
Explain how prokaryotes store and copy their genetic material
Explain why small size suits prokaryotic life
sections: The parts of a prokaryotic cell

lessons.title: Eukaryotic cells
lessons.lead: Eukaryotic cells, found in animals, plants, fungi and protists, keep their DNA in a nucleus and divide their interior into membrane-bound compartments. This compartmentalisation lets them grow larger and do many incompatible jobs at once.
objectives: Describe the main features that define a eukaryotic cell
Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
Outline the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts

lessons.title: Animal cells
lessons.lead: Animal cells are eukaryotic cells without a cell wall or chloroplasts. Their flexible membranes, lysosomes and centrioles suit the active, varied lives of animal tissues.
objectives: Identify the main structures of an animal cell and state their functions
Explain how the lack of a cell wall affects animal cells
Relate cell structure to function in a named animal cell
sections: The structures of an animal cell

lessons.title: Plant cells
lessons.lead: Plant cells share the eukaryotic plan with animal cells but add three features: a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Together these let plants make their own food and stand upright without a skeleton.
objectives: Describe the features that distinguish plant cells
Explain how the wall and vacuole keep a plant cell turgid
Explain how plasmodesmata connect plant cells

lessons.title: Fungal cells
lessons.lead: Fungi, including yeasts, moulds and mushrooms, are eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin rather than cellulose. They feed by digesting food outside their bodies and absorbing the products, and many grow as networks of thread-like hyphae.
objectives: Describe the structure of fungal cells and hyphae
Explain how fungi obtain their nutrients
Compare fungal cells with plant and animal cells

lessons.title: Bacterial cells
lessons.lead: Bacteria are the most familiar prokaryotes. Their cell walls, built from peptidoglycan, come in two main designs that the Gram stain tells apart, and these differences matter for how we treat bacterial infections.
objectives: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell wall and its function
Explain the difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria
Explain why some antibiotics damage bacteria but not human cells

lessons.title: Cell organelles
lessons.lead: Organelles are the specialised compartments and structures inside eukaryotic cells. This lesson surveys them as a system: which make things, which process and ship them, which supply energy and which recycle, and how they depend on each other.
objectives: Name the main eukaryotic organelles and state the function of each
Group organelles into the endomembrane system, energy organelles and others
Trace how organelles cooperate to make and secrete a protein

lessons.title: Nucleus and nucleolus
lessons.lead: The nucleus holds almost all of a eukaryotic cell's DNA and controls which genes are used. Inside it, the nucleolus builds the ribosomes the cell needs to make proteins.
objectives: Describe the structure of the nucleus, including the envelope and nuclear pores
Explain how DNA is packaged as chromatin
State the function of the nucleolus

lessons.title: Mitochondria
lessons.lead: Mitochondria are the organelles where aerobic respiration releases most of the energy in food, storing it as ATP. Their folded inner membrane, their own DNA and their bacterial ancestry make them one of the cell's most distinctive organelles.
objectives: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion and relate it to function
State where the stages of aerobic respiration take place
Explain why cells differ in how many mitochondria they contain

lessons.title: Chloroplasts
lessons.lead: Chloroplasts are the organelles of photosynthesis in plants and algae. They capture light energy and use it to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
objectives: Describe the structure of a chloroplast
State where the light-dependent and light-independent reactions take place
Relate the distribution of chloroplasts to their function in a leaf

lessons.title: Ribosomes
lessons.lead: Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories: they read the code in messenger RNA and join amino acids in the order it specifies. Every cell has them, and differences between bacterial and human ribosomes are the target of many antibiotics.
objectives: Describe the structure of a ribosome
Distinguish free and membrane-bound ribosomes and their products
Explain the difference between 70S and 80S ribosomes and why it matters

lessons.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
lessons.lead: The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes spreading through the cytoplasm from the nuclear envelope. Its rough parts make and fold proteins for export and membranes; its smooth parts make lipids, detoxify drugs and store calcium.
objectives: Describe the structure of rough and smooth ER
State the functions of each
Relate the amount of each type of ER to a cell's function
sections: Smooth ER: lipids, detoxification and calcium

lessons.title: Golgi apparatus
lessons.lead: The Golgi apparatus is the cell's processing and dispatch centre. It receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies them, sorts them by destination and sends them on in vesicles.
objectives: Describe the structure of the Golgi apparatus
Explain how it modifies and sorts proteins
Explain how lysosomal enzymes are targeted to lysosomes

lessons.title: Lysosomes and peroxisomes
lessons.lead: Lysosomes and peroxisomes are small membrane-bound organelles that break things down. Lysosomes digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material with acid enzymes; peroxisomes oxidise fatty acids and destroy the hydrogen peroxide this produces.
objectives: Describe the structure and functions of lysosomes
Describe the functions of peroxisomes
Explain how faults in these organelles cause disease

lessons.title: Cytoskeleton
lessons.lead: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments that gives the cell its shape, holds organelles in place, moves materials around and lets cells crawl, contract and divide. It is made of three kinds of filament with different jobs.
objectives: Describe the three types of cytoskeletal filament
Explain how motor proteins move cargo and cells
Describe the structure and function of cilia and flagella in eukaryotes

lessons.title: Cell membranes
lessons.lead: Every cell is bounded by a plasma membrane, and eukaryotic cells are full of internal membranes too. This lesson covers what membranes do: separate, control, communicate and provide surfaces where reactions happen.
objectives: List the functions of membranes in cells
Explain what is meant by partially permeable
Explain why internal membranes matter in eukaryotic cells

lessons.title: Membrane structure
lessons.lead: Membranes are built from a double layer of phospholipids with proteins floating in it, a structure described by the fluid mosaic model. This lesson explains how the parts fit together and why the structure behaves as it does.
objectives: Describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure
Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer in water
Describe the roles of cholesterol, proteins and carbohydrates in membranes

lessons.title: Membrane transport
lessons.lead: Substances cross membranes in several ways, which differ in whether they need energy and whether they need a protein. This lesson gives an overview that the following lessons explore one by one.
objectives: Distinguish passive from active transport
Choose the transport mechanism a given substance is likely to use
Explain how the size, charge and polarity of a molecule affect how it crosses a membrane

lessons.title: Diffusion
lessons.lead: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated, driven by their random motion. It is how oxygen reaches your cells and carbon dioxide leaves them, and it explains why exchange surfaces look the way they do.
objectives: Define diffusion and explain it in terms of particle movement
State the factors that affect the rate of diffusion
Calculate surface area to volume ratios and explain their significance

lessons.title: Osmosis
lessons.lead: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane. It decides whether cells swell, shrink or keep their shape, and it is described precisely using water potential.
objectives: Define osmosis in terms of water potential
Predict the effects of different solutions on animal and plant cells
Calculate water potential from solute and pressure potentials

lessons.title: Facilitated diffusion
lessons.lead: Facilitated diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient through specific membrane proteins. It lets ions and polar molecules cross membranes quickly without the cell spending energy.
objectives: Explain how channel and carrier proteins allow facilitated diffusion
Compare facilitated diffusion with simple diffusion
Explain why the rate of facilitated diffusion levels off
sections: How it differs from simple diffusion

lessons.title: Active transport
lessons.lead: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy, usually from ATP. It lets cells take up scarce nutrients, keep ion gradients that power nerves and other transport, and excrete wastes.
objectives: Explain how active transport works using carrier proteins and ATP
Describe the sodium–potassium pump
Explain co-transport, using the absorption of glucose as an example

lessons.title: Endocytosis and exocytosis
lessons.lead: Some cargo is far too large for channels or carriers. Cells take in large particles and fluid by wrapping them in membrane (endocytosis) and release large molecules by fusing vesicles with the membrane (exocytosis).
objectives: Describe phagocytosis, pinocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis
Describe exocytosis and give examples
Explain why bulk transport needs energy

lessons.title: Cell specialisation
lessons.lead: In a multicellular organism, cells take on different shapes and contents to do particular jobs. This lesson looks at how the structure of specialised cells fits their function, in animals and plants.
objectives: Explain what is meant by a specialised cell
Relate the structure of named animal and plant cells to their functions
Explain the advantages and costs of specialisation

lessons.title: Stem cells
lessons.lead: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide to renew themselves and can also give rise to specialised cells. They build the body in development, repair it in adult life, and hold great promise, and some controversy, in medicine.
objectives: Define a stem cell and describe its two key properties
Distinguish totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent stem cells
Describe medical uses of stem cells and the issues they raise

lessons.title: Cell differentiation
lessons.lead: Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised. Because nearly all cells contain the same genes, differentiation depends on switching particular genes on and off, under the control of signals and transcription factors.
objectives: Explain differentiation in terms of differential gene expression
Describe how transcription factors and signals control differentiation
Describe the evidence that differentiated cells keep their full genome

lessons.title: Cell signalling
lessons.lead: Cells constantly send and receive chemical signals that coordinate growth, metabolism and defence. A signal is detected by a receptor and converted into a response inside the cell, often amplified many times on the way.
objectives: Describe the main types of cell signalling by the distance signals travel
Distinguish cell-surface and intracellular receptors
Explain how a second messenger amplifies a signal

lessons.title: Cell junctions
lessons.lead: In tissues, cells are physically joined to their neighbours. Different junctions seal gaps, hold cells together against pulling forces, or let small molecules pass directly from cell to cell.
objectives: Describe tight junctions, anchoring junctions and gap junctions
Relate each type of junction to the tissues where it is common
Describe plasmodesmata in plants
sections: Three kinds of junction in animals

lessons.title: Cellular organisation
lessons.lead: Multicellular organisms are organised in levels: specialised cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in organ systems. This lesson connects cell biology to the body as a whole.
objectives: Define tissue, organ and organ system with examples
Name the four main types of animal tissue and the main plant tissues
Explain why multicellular organisms need organisation

lessons.module: Water and the chemistry of life
lessons.title: Chemistry of life
lessons.lead: Living things are built from a small set of elements arranged into large, complex molecules. This lesson introduces the elements, bonds and functional groups that underpin biochemistry.
objectives: Identify the main elements found in living organisms
Describe the types of chemical bond important in biology
Recognise key functional groups in biological molecules

lessons.module: Water and the chemistry of life
lessons.title: Water and biological systems
lessons.lead: Water makes up most of the mass of cells, and its unusual properties make life possible. This lesson explains how water's structure gives rise to properties that matter for organisms.
objectives: Explain why water is a polar molecule
Describe the properties of water that are important for life
Relate water's properties to examples in organisms and habitats

lessons.module: Water and the chemistry of life
lessons.title: Hydrogen bonding
lessons.lead: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions, yet they shape water, proteins and DNA. This lesson explains what hydrogen bonds are and why they are so important in biology.
objectives: Describe how hydrogen bonds form
Compare hydrogen bonds with covalent and ionic bonds
Explain the roles of hydrogen bonds in biological molecules

lessons.module: Water and the chemistry of life
lessons.title: pH and biological buffers
lessons.lead: The pH of body fluids and cells must stay within narrow limits. This lesson explains pH, acids and bases, and how buffers resist changes in pH.
objectives: Define pH and calculate it from hydrogen ion concentration
Explain how buffers resist changes in pH
Describe important biological buffer systems

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.lead: Carbohydrates provide energy, store energy and build structures. This lesson gives an overview of carbohydrate classes and their roles.
objectives: Describe the general structure and formula of carbohydrates
Classify carbohydrates into monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides
Relate carbohydrate structure to functions in organisms

lessons.title: Monosaccharides
lessons.lead: Monosaccharides are the building blocks of all carbohydrates. This lesson describes their structure, isomers and ring forms.
objectives: Classify monosaccharides by number of carbons and functional group
Distinguish α-glucose from β-glucose
Explain the roles of important monosaccharides
sections: Ring forms and α and β glucose

lessons.title: Disaccharides
lessons.lead: Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a glycosidic bond. This lesson covers how they form and the main examples.
objectives: Describe the formation and breakdown of glycosidic bonds
Name the monomers of maltose, sucrose and lactose
Explain how to test for reducing and non-reducing sugars

lessons.title: Polysaccharides
lessons.lead: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugar units used for storage and structure. This lesson compares starch, glycogen and cellulose and relates their structures to their functions.
objectives: Describe the structures of amylose, amylopectin and glycogen
Describe the structure of cellulose
Explain how each structure suits its function

lessons.title: Lipids
lessons.lead: Lipids are a diverse group of molecules that are insoluble in water. This lesson introduces their main types and functions.
objectives: Describe the general properties of lipids
Identify the main classes of lipid
Describe the functions of lipids in organisms

lessons.title: Fatty acids
lessons.lead: Fatty acids are the main components of triglycerides and phospholipids. This lesson explains their structure and the differences between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.
objectives: Describe the structure of a fatty acid
Distinguish saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids
Explain how fatty acid structure affects melting point and health

lessons.title: Triglycerides
lessons.lead: Triglycerides are the main form of stored fat in plants and animals. This lesson explains how they form and why they are effective energy stores.
objectives: Describe the structure and formation of a triglyceride
Explain why triglycerides are good energy stores
Describe other functions of triglycerides

lessons.title: Phospholipids
lessons.lead: Phospholipids form the basic structure of all cell membranes. This lesson explains their structure and how they arrange themselves in water.
objectives: Describe the structure of a phospholipid
Explain how phospholipids form bilayers in water
Relate phospholipid properties to membrane function

lessons.title: Steroids
lessons.lead: Steroids are lipids with a ring structure rather than fatty acid chains. This lesson describes their structure and important examples such as cholesterol and steroid hormones.
objectives: Describe the basic structure of steroids
Explain the roles of cholesterol in cells
Describe how steroid hormones act

lessons.title: Proteins
lessons.lead: Proteins carry out most of the work in cells, from catalysis to transport and structure. This lesson gives an overview of protein functions and the levels of protein structure.
objectives: Describe the range of functions carried out by proteins
Outline the four levels of protein structure
Distinguish globular and fibrous proteins

lessons.title: Amino acids
lessons.lead: Amino acids are the monomers of proteins. This lesson describes their structure, classification and properties.
objectives: Describe the general structure of an amino acid
Classify amino acids by their R groups
Explain how amino acids behave in solution

lessons.title: Peptide bonds
lessons.lead: Amino acids join through peptide bonds to form polypeptides. This lesson explains how peptide bonds form and break and why the polypeptide backbone has directional ends.
objectives: Describe the formation of a peptide bond by condensation
Explain the hydrolysis of peptide bonds
Describe the properties of the polypeptide backbone

lessons.title: Protein primary structure
lessons.lead: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. This lesson explains why sequence determines a protein's shape and function.
objectives: Define primary structure
Explain how primary structure determines higher levels of structure
Describe how changes in primary structure affect function

lessons.title: Protein secondary structure
lessons.lead: Secondary structure is the regular folding of the polypeptide backbone into helices and sheets. This lesson describes α-helices and β-pleated sheets and how they are stabilised.
objectives: Describe the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet
Explain how hydrogen bonds stabilise secondary structure
Give examples of proteins rich in each type

lessons.title: Protein tertiary structure
lessons.lead: Tertiary structure is the overall 3D shape of a single polypeptide. This lesson explains the bonds and interactions that hold it and why it matters for function.
objectives: Define tertiary structure
Describe the bonds and interactions that stabilise tertiary structure
Relate tertiary structure to protein function

lessons.title: Protein quaternary structure
lessons.lead: Some proteins are made of more than one polypeptide chain. This lesson explains quaternary structure, using haemoglobin and collagen as examples.
objectives: Define quaternary structure
Describe the quaternary structure of haemoglobin and collagen
Explain the role of prosthetic groups in conjugated proteins

lessons.title: Protein folding
lessons.lead: Newly made polypeptides must fold into precise shapes to function. This lesson explains how proteins fold, how cells help and what happens when folding goes wrong.
objectives: Explain the principle that sequence determines folding
Describe the role of chaperones in protein folding
Explain consequences of misfolding, including disease

lessons.title: Protein denaturation
lessons.lead: Denaturation is the loss of a protein's 3D shape and function. This lesson explains what causes denaturation and why it matters.
objectives: Define denaturation
Explain how temperature, pH and chemicals cause denaturation
Explain the consequences of denaturation for function

lessons.title: Enzymes
lessons.lead: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions in living cells. This lesson explains what enzymes are, how they lower activation energy and where they work.
objectives: Define enzymes as biological catalysts
Explain how enzymes lower activation energy
Distinguish intracellular and extracellular enzymes

lessons.title: Enzyme-substrate interactions
lessons.lead: Enzymes bind their substrates with great specificity. This lesson explains the lock and key and induced fit models and how enzyme-substrate complexes lead to products.
objectives: Describe the formation of enzyme-substrate complexes
Compare the lock and key and induced fit models
Explain enzyme specificity

lessons.title: Enzyme kinetics
lessons.lead: Enzyme kinetics describes how reaction rate depends on substrate concentration. This lesson introduces Vmax, Km and the Michaelis-Menten relationship.
objectives: Describe how reaction rate changes with substrate concentration
Define Vmax and Km
Interpret enzyme kinetics graphs

lessons.title: Enzyme inhibition
lessons.lead: Inhibitors reduce enzyme activity and are important in metabolic control and medicine. This lesson compares competitive, non-competitive and irreversible inhibition.
objectives: Distinguish competitive and non-competitive inhibition
Explain the effects of inhibitors on Vmax and Km
Describe the roles of inhibitors in metabolism and medicine

lessons.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity
lessons.lead: Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration. This lesson explains each factor and how to investigate them.
objectives: Explain the effects of temperature and pH on enzyme activity
Explain the effects of substrate and enzyme concentration
Describe how to investigate enzyme activity in the laboratory

lessons.title: Nucleic acids
lessons.lead: Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information. This lesson describes nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA and RNA, and how they link together.
objectives: Describe the structure of a nucleotide
Explain how nucleotides join to form polynucleotides
Distinguish purines and pyrimidines

lessons.title: DNA and RNA
lessons.lead: DNA and RNA are both nucleic acids but differ in structure and role. This lesson compares them and explains DNA's double helix and base pairing.
objectives: Describe the double helix structure of DNA
Explain complementary base pairing
Compare the structures and functions of DNA and RNA

lessons.title: ATP and biological energy
lessons.lead: ATP is the main energy currency of cells. This lesson explains its structure, how it releases energy and how it is regenerated.
objectives: Describe the structure of ATP
Explain how ATP hydrolysis releases energy for cellular processes
Describe how ATP is resynthesised

lessons.title: Introduction to genetics
lessons.lead: Genetics is the study of genes, heredity and variation. This lesson introduces the core ideas and key milestones of genetics.
objectives: Define genetics, heredity and variation
Describe the relationship between DNA, genes and proteins
Outline key milestones in the history of genetics

lessons.title: DNA structure
lessons.lead: The structure of DNA explains how it stores and copies genetic information. This lesson focuses on the evidence for the double helix and how structure relates to function.
objectives: Describe the evidence used to determine DNA structure
Explain how DNA's structure allows information storage
Explain how DNA's structure allows accurate copying

lessons.title: DNA replication
lessons.lead: Before a cell divides, its DNA must be copied accurately. This lesson explains semi-conservative replication and the enzymes involved.
objectives: Describe semi-conservative replication and its evidence
Explain the roles of key enzymes in replication
Explain leading and lagging strand synthesis

lessons.title: DNA repair
lessons.lead: DNA is constantly damaged and must be repaired to keep genetic information intact. This lesson describes the main repair mechanisms and the consequences of failure.
objectives: Describe proofreading and mismatch repair
Describe excision repair and double-strand break repair
Explain the consequences of defective DNA repair

lessons.title: Chromosomes
lessons.lead: Chromosomes package DNA so that it fits in cells and can be divided accurately. This lesson describes chromosome structure and organisation in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
objectives: Describe how DNA is packaged into chromosomes in eukaryotes
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic chromosomes
Describe the human karyotype

lessons.title: Genes and alleles
lessons.lead: Genes come in different versions called alleles. This lesson explains genes, alleles and loci, and how alleles create variation.
objectives: Define gene, allele and locus
Distinguish homozygous and heterozygous genotypes
Explain how new alleles arise and contribute to variation

lessons.title: Genomes
lessons.lead: A genome is all the genetic material of an organism. This lesson compares genome sizes and structures and explains what makes up the human genome.
objectives: Define genome and describe genome size
Describe the composition of the human genome
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes

lessons.title: RNA structure
lessons.lead: RNA molecules fold into shapes that suit their roles in gene expression. This lesson describes the structures of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
objectives: Describe the structure of mRNA
Describe the structure of tRNA and how it carries amino acids
Describe the role and structure of rRNA in ribosomes

lessons.title: Transcription
lessons.lead: Transcription copies the information in a gene into RNA. This lesson explains how RNA polymerase makes mRNA from a DNA template.
objectives: Describe the stages of transcription
Explain the roles of RNA polymerase, promoters and template strands
Compare transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes

lessons.title: RNA processing
lessons.lead: In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA must be processed before it can be translated. This lesson explains capping, splicing and polyadenylation.
objectives: Describe capping and polyadenylation of pre-mRNA
Explain splicing of introns and exons
Explain how alternative splicing increases protein diversity

lessons.title: Translation
lessons.lead: Translation converts the code in mRNA into a sequence of amino acids. This lesson describes the stages of translation on ribosomes.
objectives: Describe the structure of the ribosome and its sites
Explain initiation, elongation and termination of translation
Explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA and ribosomes

lessons.title: Genetic code
lessons.lead: The genetic code is the set of rules linking codons to amino acids. This lesson explains its key features.
objectives: Describe the triplet nature of the genetic code
Explain degeneracy, universality and non-overlapping features
Use a codon table to translate sequences

lessons.title: Protein synthesis
lessons.lead: Protein synthesis brings together transcription, processing and translation. This lesson follows a protein from gene to final functional form.
objectives: Summarise the stages of protein synthesis from gene to protein
Describe post-translational modification and protein targeting
Explain how proteins reach their final locations

lessons.title: Gene regulation
lessons.lead: Cells control which genes are expressed, when and how much. This lesson explains the main levels of gene regulation in eukaryotes.
objectives: Explain why gene regulation is necessary
Describe regulation at the level of transcription
Describe regulation after transcription

lessons.title: Operons
lessons.lead: In bacteria, genes for related functions are often grouped in operons and controlled together. This lesson explains the lac operon as a model of gene regulation.
objectives: Describe the structure of an operon
Explain how the lac operon is regulated by lactose
Explain the role of glucose and catabolite activation

lessons.title: Epigenetics
lessons.lead: Epigenetic changes alter gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. This lesson explains DNA methylation, histone modification and their effects.
objectives: Define epigenetics
Describe DNA methylation and histone modification
Explain examples of epigenetic effects in development and disease

lessons.title: Mutations
lessons.lead: Mutations are changes in DNA sequence. This lesson explains how mutations arise, where they occur and why they matter.
objectives: Define mutation and distinguish somatic and germline mutations
Describe causes of mutation
Explain the possible effects of mutations

lessons.title: Types of mutation
lessons.lead: Gene mutations take several forms, with very different consequences. This lesson compares substitutions, insertions and deletions and their effects on proteins.
objectives: Describe substitution, insertion and deletion mutations
Distinguish silent, missense and nonsense mutations
Explain the effects of frameshift mutations

lessons.title: DNA damage
lessons.lead: DNA is damaged thousands of times a day in every cell. This lesson describes the main sources and types of DNA damage and how damage leads to mutation.
objectives: Identify endogenous and environmental sources of DNA damage
Describe common types of DNA damage
Explain how unrepaired damage becomes a mutation

lessons.title: Mendelian genetics
lessons.lead: Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants revealed the basic rules of inheritance. This lesson explains his methods and his laws.
objectives: Describe Mendel's experimental approach
State Mendel's law of segregation
State Mendel's law of independent assortment

lessons.title: Dominant and recessive inheritance
lessons.lead: Some alleles mask others in heterozygotes. This lesson explains dominant and recessive alleles and autosomal inheritance patterns in humans.
objectives: Define dominant and recessive alleles
Describe autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance patterns
Explain carriers and the probability of inheriting recessive conditions

lessons.title: Genotype and phenotype
lessons.lead: Genotype describes the alleles an organism has, while phenotype describes its characteristics. This lesson explains the relationship between them and the role of environment.
objectives: Define genotype and phenotype
Explain how genotype and environment together determine phenotype
Distinguish discontinuous and continuous variation

lessons.title: Monohybrid crosses
lessons.lead: A monohybrid cross follows the inheritance of one gene. This lesson shows how to use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares and how to predict ratios.
objectives: Construct genetic diagrams and Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses
Predict genotype and phenotype ratios
Use a test cross to determine an unknown genotype

lessons.title: Dihybrid crosses
lessons.lead: A dihybrid cross follows two genes at once. This lesson explains how independent assortment produces the 9:3:3:1 ratio.
objectives: Determine gametes for a dihybrid cross
Construct a Punnett square for a dihybrid cross
Explain deviations from expected dihybrid ratios

lessons.title: Incomplete dominance
lessons.lead: In incomplete dominance, heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype. This lesson explains how it works and how it changes ratios.
objectives: Define incomplete dominance
Predict ratios from crosses with incomplete dominance
Explain incomplete dominance at the molecular level

lessons.title: Codominance
lessons.lead: In codominance, both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed. This lesson explains codominance with blood group and other examples.
objectives: Define codominance
Explain the ABO blood group system as codominance and multiple alleles
Predict offspring blood groups from parental genotypes

lessons.title: Sex-linked inheritance
lessons.lead: Genes on the sex chromosomes are inherited differently in males and females. This lesson explains X-linked inheritance and conditions such as haemophilia.
objectives: Explain how sex is determined in humans
Describe X-linked recessive inheritance
Predict outcomes of crosses involving X-linked genes

lessons.title: Pedigree analysis
lessons.lead: Pedigrees show how a trait is passed through a family. This lesson explains how to read pedigrees and identify inheritance patterns.
objectives: Interpret standard pedigree symbols
Identify autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked patterns
Deduce genotypes and probabilities from pedigrees

lessons.title: Population genetics
lessons.lead: Population genetics studies how allele frequencies vary and change in populations. This lesson introduces allele frequencies and the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
objectives: Calculate allele and genotype frequencies
State and apply the Hardy-Weinberg equation
Explain the conditions required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

lessons.title: Genetic linkage
lessons.lead: Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This lesson explains linkage and how it alters expected ratios.
objectives: Define genetic linkage
Explain how linkage changes the results of dihybrid crosses
Use recombination frequency to estimate distances between genes

lessons.title: Recombination
lessons.lead: Recombination creates new combinations of alleles. This lesson explains crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis and their role in variation.
objectives: Describe crossing over in prophase I of meiosis
Explain independent assortment of homologous chromosomes
Explain how recombination and fertilisation generate genetic variation

lessons.title: Chromosomal abnormalities
lessons.lead: Changes in chromosome number or structure can have major effects on development. This lesson explains how they arise and gives important examples.
objectives: Explain how non-disjunction causes changes in chromosome number
Describe examples of aneuploidy in humans
Describe structural chromosome changes

lessons.title: Genomics
lessons.lead: Genomics studies whole genomes, using sequencing and computing. This lesson explains how genomes are sequenced and what genomics is used for.
objectives: Describe methods of DNA sequencing
Explain the main applications of genomics
Discuss ethical issues in genomics

lessons.title: Human genetic variation
lessons.lead: Humans differ from one another at millions of positions in the genome. This lesson describes the types of human genetic variation and what they reveal.
objectives: Describe types of human genetic variation
Explain patterns of variation within and between populations
Explain how human variation reveals our evolutionary history

lessons.title: Genome-wide association studies
lessons.lead: Genome-wide association studies scan the genome for variants linked to traits and diseases. This lesson explains how GWAS work, what they find and their limitations.
objectives: Describe how a genome-wide association study is carried out
Interpret GWAS results, including Manhattan plots
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of GWAS

lessons.title: Cell cycle
lessons.lead: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell grows and divides. This lesson outlines its phases and why it matters.
objectives: Describe the phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle
Explain what happens to DNA content during the cycle
Explain the importance of the cell cycle for growth and repair

lessons.title: Interphase
lessons.lead: Interphase is the longest part of the cell cycle and prepares the cell for division. This lesson explains what happens in each stage of interphase.
objectives: Describe events in G₁, S and G₂
Explain why interphase is needed before division
Relate interphase activities to successful mitosis

lessons.title: Mitosis
lessons.lead: Mitosis divides the nucleus to produce two genetically identical nuclei. This lesson describes its stages and the role of the spindle.
objectives: Describe the stages of mitosis
Explain the role of spindle fibres and centromeres
Describe cytokinesis in animal and plant cells

lessons.title: Meiosis
lessons.lead: Meiosis is the division that produces gametes with half the chromosome number. This lesson outlines the two divisions of meiosis.
objectives: Describe the main events of meiosis I and meiosis II
Explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number
Explain why meiosis is needed in sexual reproduction

lessons.title: Comparison of mitosis and meiosis
lessons.lead: Mitosis and meiosis are both forms of nuclear division but have different outcomes and roles. This lesson compares them directly.
objectives: Compare the processes of mitosis and meiosis
Compare the products of mitosis and meiosis
Relate each type of division to its role in organisms

lessons.title: Chromosome segregation
lessons.lead: Accurate chromosome segregation ensures each daughter cell receives the correct chromosomes. This lesson explains how cells achieve this and what happens when it fails.
objectives: Explain the role of cohesin and the spindle in segregation
Describe the spindle assembly checkpoint
Explain the consequences of segregation errors

lessons.title: Cell-cycle regulation
lessons.lead: The cell cycle is controlled by proteins that drive cells from one phase to the next. This lesson explains the roles of cyclins, CDKs and growth signals.
objectives: Describe the roles of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases
Explain how growth factors stimulate division
Explain how proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes regulate the cycle

lessons.title: Checkpoints
lessons.lead: Checkpoints are control points where the cell checks whether conditions are right to continue the cycle. This lesson explains the main checkpoints and the role of p53.
objectives: Describe the G₁, G₂ and metaphase checkpoints
Explain the role of p53 in responding to DNA damage
Explain the consequences of checkpoint failure

lessons.title: Apoptosis
lessons.lead: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a controlled process that removes unwanted cells. This lesson explains how it happens and why it is important.
objectives: Describe the features of apoptosis
Explain the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis
Explain the roles of apoptosis in development and disease

lessons.title: Necrosis
lessons.lead: Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death caused by injury or damage. This lesson compares necrosis with apoptosis and describes its effects.
objectives: Describe the features of necrosis
Compare necrosis with apoptosis
Explain the causes and consequences of necrosis

lessons.title: Cellular senescence
lessons.lead: Senescent cells stop dividing permanently but remain alive. This lesson explains why cells become senescent and the role of telomeres.
objectives: Define cellular senescence
Explain how telomere shortening limits cell division
Describe the roles of senescence in ageing and cancer protection

lessons.title: Cancer biology
lessons.lead: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division caused by changes in genes that regulate the cell cycle. This lesson explains the genetic basis and hallmarks of cancer.
objectives: Explain how mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes cause cancer
Describe the hallmarks of cancer
Identify risk factors for cancer

lessons.title: Tumour development
lessons.lead: Tumours develop in stages from a single altered cell to an invasive cancer. This lesson describes benign and malignant tumours and the process of metastasis.
objectives: Distinguish benign and malignant tumours
Describe the stages of tumour progression
Explain how metastasis occurs

lessons.title: Stem-cell biology
lessons.lead: Stem cells can divide to renew themselves and differentiate into specialised cells. This lesson explains types of stem cells and their uses.
objectives: Define stem cells and their key properties
Distinguish totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent stem cells
Describe uses and ethical issues of stem cells

lessons.title: Embryonic development
lessons.lead: Embryonic development turns a single cell into a complex organism. This lesson outlines the main stages and processes involved.
objectives: Outline the main stages of animal embryonic development
Describe the key processes of development
Explain how development is controlled by genes

lessons.title: Fertilisation
lessons.lead: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm and egg to form a zygote. This lesson explains the steps of fertilisation in mammals and how only one sperm enters.
objectives: Describe the acrosome reaction and sperm-egg fusion
Explain how polyspermy is prevented
Explain the significance of fertilisation for chromosome number and development

lessons.title: Cleavage
lessons.lead: Cleavage is the series of rapid cell divisions that follows fertilisation. This lesson describes how cleavage forms the blastula and the mammalian blastocyst.
objectives: Describe the features of cleavage divisions
Describe the formation of the morula, blastula and blastocyst
Explain the significance of the inner cell mass and trophoblast

lessons.title: Gastrulation
lessons.lead: Gastrulation reorganises the embryo into germ layers, setting up the body plan. This lesson describes the germ layers and what they form.
objectives: Describe the process of gastrulation
Name the three germ layers and the tissues they form
Explain the significance of gastrulation for the body plan

lessons.title: Organogenesis
lessons.lead: Organogenesis is the formation of organs from the germ layers. This lesson describes neurulation and other examples of organ formation.
objectives: Describe neurulation and the formation of the neural tube
Explain how organs form through interactions between tissues
Explain the vulnerability of organogenesis to disruption

lessons.title: Developmental signalling
lessons.lead: Cells in an embryo communicate using signalling molecules that control their fates. This lesson explains morphogens and major signalling pathways.
objectives: Explain how morphogen gradients specify cell fates
Describe major developmental signalling pathways
Explain the consequences of faulty developmental signalling

lessons.title: Cell fate determination
lessons.lead: During development, cells become committed to particular fates. This lesson explains specification, determination and the factors that decide cell fate.
objectives: Distinguish specification, determination and differentiation
Explain how cytoplasmic determinants and signals influence fate
Describe how transcription factors lock in cell identity

lessons.title: Tissue formation
lessons.lead: Tissues form as cells of similar types organise and adhere together. This lesson describes the main animal tissue types and how cells build them.
objectives: Describe the four main types of animal tissue
Explain the roles of cell adhesion and the extracellular matrix
Explain how tissues combine to form organs

lessons.title: Regeneration
lessons.lead: Some animals can regrow lost body parts, while others, including humans, have limited regeneration. This lesson compares regenerative abilities and their mechanisms.
objectives: Describe examples of regeneration in different animals
Explain the mechanisms of regeneration, including blastema formation
Explain why regeneration is limited in mammals and its medical potential

lessons.title: Origins of evolutionary thought
lessons.lead: Ideas about how species change developed over centuries before and after Darwin. This lesson traces key thinkers and how evolutionary theory emerged.
objectives: Describe early ideas about the diversity of life
Compare Lamarck's ideas with Darwin and Wallace's theory
Explain how the modern synthesis combined evolution and genetics

lessons.title: Evidence for evolution
lessons.lead: Evolution is supported by many independent lines of evidence. This lesson summarises the main types of evidence.
objectives: Describe fossil and anatomical evidence for evolution
Describe molecular and biogeographical evidence
Explain how observed evolution supports the theory

lessons.title: Natural selection
lessons.lead: Natural selection is the main mechanism of adaptive evolution. This lesson explains how it works step by step.
objectives: State the conditions needed for natural selection
Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies
Describe directional, stabilising and disruptive selection

lessons.title: Adaptation
lessons.lead: Adaptations are inherited features that improve survival and reproduction in a particular environment. This lesson describes types of adaptation and how they evolve.
objectives: Define adaptation
Distinguish anatomical, physiological and behavioural adaptations
Explain how adaptations arise by natural selection

lessons.title: Genetic variation
lessons.lead: Genetic variation is the raw material for evolution. This lesson explains its sources and how it is measured and maintained.
objectives: Describe the sources of genetic variation
Explain how genetic variation can be measured in populations
Explain how variation is maintained in populations

lessons.title: Mutation and evolution
lessons.lead: Mutations provide the new genetic variation on which evolution depends. This lesson explains the role of mutation in evolution.
objectives: Explain why mutation is essential for evolution
Describe the range of fitness effects of mutations
Explain how mutation rate and population size affect evolution

lessons.title: Genetic drift
lessons.lead: Genetic drift is change in allele frequencies due to chance. This lesson explains drift and its strong effects in small populations.
objectives: Define genetic drift
Explain the bottleneck and founder effects
Compare drift with natural selection

lessons.title: Gene flow
lessons.lead: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations. This lesson explains how gene flow affects variation and divergence.
objectives: Define gene flow
Explain how gene flow affects genetic variation within and between populations
Describe the role of gene flow in conservation and speciation

lessons.title: Sexual selection
lessons.lead: Sexual selection favours traits that improve mating success. This lesson explains intrasexual and intersexual selection and their results.
objectives: Define sexual selection
Distinguish intrasexual and intersexual selection
Explain why sexual selection can favour costly traits

lessons.title: Selection pressures
lessons.lead: Selection pressures are environmental factors that affect survival and reproduction. This lesson explains biotic and abiotic pressures and how they drive evolution.
objectives: Define selection pressure
Distinguish biotic and abiotic selection pressures
Explain how changing selection pressures drive evolution

lessons.title: Fitness
lessons.lead: In evolutionary biology, fitness means reproductive success, not physical strength. This lesson explains how fitness is defined and measured.
objectives: Define biological fitness
Distinguish absolute and relative fitness
Explain inclusive fitness and kin selection

lessons.title: Speciation
lessons.lead: Speciation is the formation of new species. This lesson explains the biological species concept and the general process of speciation.
objectives: Define a species using the biological species concept
Explain the general process of speciation
Describe limitations of the biological species concept

lessons.title: Reproductive isolation
lessons.lead: Reproductive isolation keeps species separate. This lesson explains prezygotic and postzygotic barriers.
objectives: Describe prezygotic isolating mechanisms
Describe postzygotic isolating mechanisms
Explain how reproductive isolation completes speciation

lessons.title: Allopatric speciation
lessons.lead: Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are geographically separated. This lesson explains how geographic isolation leads to new species.
objectives: Define allopatric speciation
Explain how geographic isolation leads to reproductive isolation
Describe examples of allopatric speciation

lessons.title: Sympatric speciation
lessons.lead: Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic separation. This lesson explains how new species can form within the same area.
objectives: Define sympatric speciation
Explain speciation by polyploidy
Explain speciation by ecological and behavioural divergence

lessons.title: Phylogenetics
lessons.lead: Phylogenetics reconstructs the evolutionary relationships between organisms. This lesson explains the data and methods used.
objectives: Define phylogeny and phylogenetics
Describe the types of evidence used in phylogenetics
Explain the principle of parsimony and shared derived characters

lessons.title: Evolutionary trees
lessons.lead: Evolutionary trees show relationships between groups of organisms. This lesson explains how to read them correctly.
objectives: Identify the parts of an evolutionary tree
Interpret relationships from branching patterns
Avoid common misreadings of evolutionary trees

lessons.title: Common ancestry
lessons.lead: All living organisms share a common ancestor. This lesson explains the evidence for universal common ancestry and what we can infer about it.
objectives: Explain the idea of universal common ancestry
Describe evidence for a last universal common ancestor
Describe the three domains of life

lessons.title: Fossil evidence
lessons.lead: Fossils provide direct evidence of past life and evolutionary change. This lesson explains how fossils form, how they are dated and what they show.
objectives: Describe how fossils form
Explain how fossils and rocks are dated
Explain the strengths and limitations of the fossil record

lessons.title: Molecular evolution
lessons.lead: Molecular evolution studies how DNA and protein sequences change over time. This lesson explains the neutral theory and molecular clocks.
objectives: Explain how sequence differences reveal evolutionary relationships
Describe the neutral theory of molecular evolution
Explain how molecular clocks are used to estimate divergence times

lessons.title: Human evolution
lessons.lead: Human evolution traces the hominin lineage from our common ancestor with chimpanzees to modern humans. This lesson outlines key species and evidence.
objectives: Describe key hominin species and their features
Explain the evidence for the African origin of modern humans
Describe interbreeding with archaic humans

lessons.title: Evolutionary medicine
lessons.lead: Evolutionary medicine applies evolutionary thinking to health and disease. This lesson explains how evolution helps explain why we get ill.
objectives: Explain the idea of evolutionary mismatch
Explain trade-offs and defences in evolutionary medicine
Apply evolutionary thinking to pathogens and cancer

lessons.title: Evolution of resistance
lessons.lead: Resistance to antibiotics, pesticides and other treatments evolves by natural selection. This lesson explains how resistance arises and how to slow it.
objectives: Explain how antibiotic resistance evolves
Describe how resistance genes spread between bacteria
Describe strategies to reduce the evolution of resistance

lessons.title: Population genetics
lessons.lead: Population genetics provides the mathematical framework for evolution. This lesson brings together the forces that change allele frequencies.
objectives: Identify the forces that change allele frequencies in populations
Use deviations from Hardy-Weinberg expectations to infer evolutionary forces
Explain how population genetics links to speciation and conservation

lessons.title: Organisation of the human body
lessons.lead: The human body is organised from cells into tissues, organs and organ systems. This lesson introduces that organisation and the main body systems.
objectives: Describe the levels of organisation in the human body
Name the four main tissue types
Outline the major organ systems and their roles

lessons.title: Homeostasis
lessons.lead: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable. This lesson explains negative feedback and examples of homeostatic control.
objectives: Define homeostasis
Describe the components of a negative feedback loop
Distinguish negative and positive feedback with examples

lessons.title: Nervous system
lessons.lead: The nervous system provides rapid communication throughout the body. This lesson introduces its divisions and functions.
objectives: Describe the main functions of the nervous system
Distinguish the central and peripheral nervous systems
Describe a reflex arc

lessons.title: Neurones
lessons.lead: Neurones are cells specialised to transmit electrical impulses. This lesson describes their structure and types.
objectives: Describe the structure of a neurone
Distinguish sensory, relay and motor neurones
Explain the role of myelination and glial cells

lessons.title: Action potentials
lessons.lead: An action potential is a brief electrical impulse along a neurone. This lesson explains resting potential and the stages of an action potential.
objectives: Explain how the resting potential is maintained
Describe the stages of an action potential
Explain the all-or-nothing principle and the refractory period

lessons.title: Synaptic transmission
lessons.lead: Synapses pass signals between neurones or to effectors. This lesson explains chemical synaptic transmission.
objectives: Describe the structure of a chemical synapse
Explain the sequence of events in synaptic transmission
Explain how drugs can affect synapses

lessons.title: Central nervous system
lessons.lead: The central nervous system integrates information and controls the body. This lesson describes the main regions of the brain and the spinal cord.
objectives: Describe the main regions of the brain and their functions
Describe the structure and roles of the spinal cord
Describe how the CNS is protected

lessons.title: Peripheral nervous system
lessons.lead: The peripheral nervous system connects the CNS to the rest of the body. This lesson explains its somatic and autonomic divisions.
objectives: Describe the divisions of the peripheral nervous system
Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems
Explain how the autonomic system controls organs

lessons.title: Endocrine system
lessons.lead: The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood to coordinate the body. This lesson describes the main glands and their hormones.
objectives: Describe the main endocrine glands and their hormones
Explain the role of the hypothalamus and pituitary gland
Compare endocrine and nervous control

lessons.title: Hormones and signalling
lessons.lead: Hormones signal through receptors on or inside target cells. This lesson explains how different types of hormones act.
objectives: Distinguish peptide and steroid hormones
Explain how peptide hormones act via second messengers
Explain how steroid hormones affect gene expression

lessons.title: Cardiovascular system
lessons.lead: The cardiovascular system transports substances around the body. This lesson introduces the heart, blood vessels and blood.
objectives: Describe the components of the cardiovascular system
Explain the functions of the cardiovascular system
Describe major risk factors for cardiovascular disease

lessons.title: Heart anatomy
lessons.lead: The heart is a muscular double pump. This lesson describes its chambers, valves and blood supply.
objectives: Describe the chambers and major vessels of the heart
Explain the role of the heart valves
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker wall

lessons.title: Cardiac cycle
lessons.lead: The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one heartbeat. This lesson explains its stages and how the heartbeat is controlled.
objectives: Describe the stages of the cardiac cycle
Explain how pressure changes open and close valves
Describe the electrical control of the heartbeat

lessons.title: Blood vessels
lessons.lead: Arteries, capillaries and veins have structures suited to their functions. This lesson compares them.
objectives: Describe the structure of arteries, capillaries and veins
Relate the structure of each vessel to its function
Explain how tissue fluid forms at capillaries

lessons.title: Blood composition
lessons.lead: Blood is a tissue made of cells suspended in plasma. This lesson describes its components and their functions.
objectives: Describe the components of blood
Explain the functions of red cells, white cells and platelets
Describe the ABO blood group system

lessons.title: Circulation
lessons.lead: Humans have a double circulation with pulmonary and systemic circuits. This lesson explains how circulation is organised and regulated.
objectives: Explain the double circulatory system
Describe blood pressure and how it is measured
Explain how blood flow is redistributed during exercise

lessons.title: Respiratory system
lessons.lead: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. This lesson describes its structures and protective features.
objectives: Describe the structures of the respiratory system
Explain how the airways are protected
Describe common respiratory diseases

lessons.title: Ventilation
lessons.lead: Ventilation moves air into and out of the lungs. This lesson explains the mechanism of breathing and lung volumes.
objectives: Describe the mechanism of inspiration and expiration
Define and interpret lung volumes
Explain how breathing rate is controlled

lessons.title: Gas exchange
lessons.lead: Gas exchange in the alveoli supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. This lesson explains how alveoli are adapted and what affects exchange.
objectives: Describe the adaptations of alveoli for gas exchange
Apply Fick's law to gas exchange
Explain how disease affects gas exchange

lessons.title: Oxygen transport
lessons.lead: Haemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. This lesson explains the oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr effect.
objectives: Describe how haemoglobin carries oxygen
Interpret the oxygen dissociation curve
Explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin

lessons.title: Digestive system
lessons.lead: The digestive system breaks down food and absorbs nutrients. This lesson describes the main organs and their roles.
objectives: Describe the organs of the digestive system
Distinguish mechanical and chemical digestion
Explain the roles of the stomach and the large intestine

lessons.title: Digestion and absorption
lessons.lead: Food molecules are digested into small units and absorbed in the small intestine. This lesson explains digestive enzymes and absorption.
objectives: Describe the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
Explain how the small intestine is adapted for absorption
Describe the mechanisms of absorption

lessons.title: Liver and pancreas
lessons.lead: The liver and pancreas have essential digestive and metabolic roles. This lesson describes their functions.
objectives: Describe the main functions of the liver
Describe the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas
Explain the effects of liver disease and diabetes

lessons.title: Renal system
lessons.lead: The renal system removes wastes and controls water and salt balance. This lesson describes its organs and roles.
objectives: Describe the organs of the renal system
Describe the main functions of the kidneys
Describe kidney failure and its treatment

lessons.title: Kidney function
lessons.lead: The nephron filters blood and adjusts the composition of urine. This lesson explains the structure of the nephron and how it works.
objectives: Describe the structure of the nephron
Explain ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption
Explain how ADH controls water reabsorption

lessons.title: Urine formation
lessons.lead: Urine composition reflects how the kidneys regulate the body. This lesson explains the countercurrent multiplier and what urine tests reveal.
objectives: Explain how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier
Relate urine concentration to body water balance
Interpret urine test results

lessons.title: Musculoskeletal system
lessons.lead: The musculoskeletal system supports the body and allows movement. This lesson describes the skeleton, joints and muscles.
objectives: Describe the functions of the skeleton
Describe the structure of a synovial joint
Explain how antagonistic muscles produce movement

lessons.title: Bone physiology
lessons.lead: Bone is a living tissue that is constantly remodelled. This lesson explains bone structure, growth and remodelling.
objectives: Describe the structure of compact and spongy bone
Explain the roles of osteoblasts and osteoclasts
Explain how calcium balance and bone health are regulated

lessons.title: Muscle contraction
lessons.lead: Skeletal muscle contracts by the sliding of protein filaments. This lesson explains the sliding filament theory.
objectives: Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle fibre and sarcomere
Explain the sliding filament theory
Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in contraction

lessons.title: Immune system
lessons.lead: The immune system defends the body against pathogens. This lesson introduces innate and adaptive immunity.
objectives: Describe physical and chemical barriers to infection
Distinguish innate and adaptive immunity
Describe the roles of the main immune cells

lessons.title: Reproductive system
lessons.lead: The reproductive systems produce gametes and allow fertilisation. This lesson describes male and female reproductive anatomy and the menstrual cycle.
objectives: Describe the male and female reproductive organs
Describe the hormonal control of the menstrual cycle
Describe methods of contraception and fertility treatment

lessons.title: Human development
lessons.lead: Human development continues from fertilisation through birth, childhood and ageing. This lesson describes pregnancy, birth and growth.
objectives: Describe the stages of pregnancy
Explain the role of the placenta
Describe growth and development after birth

lessons.title: Skin and thermoregulation
lessons.lead: The skin protects the body and helps control temperature. This lesson explains skin structure and thermoregulation.
objectives: Describe the structure and functions of the skin
Explain how the body responds to overheating
Explain how the body responds to cooling

lessons.title: Fluid and electrolyte balance
lessons.lead: The body controls the volume and composition of its fluids. This lesson explains water and electrolyte balance and its hormonal control.
objectives: Describe the distribution of body water
Explain the roles of key electrolytes
