resources.q: Name the five unifying ideas of biology.
resources.a: Cells, genes (inheritance), evolution, energy flow and homeostasis.

resources.q: Why does biology depend on chemistry and physics?
resources.a: Living things are made of matter and obey physical and chemical laws: enzymes are catalysts, nerve impulses are electrical, transport follows diffusion and fluid flow.

resources.q: Which statement is part of cell theory?
resources.a: Cells only arise from existing cells

resources.q: A biologist studies how the population of a bird species changes over 30 years as its habitat warms. Which level of biology is this mainly?
resources.a: Population ecology and evolution

resources.q: Which example best shows how biology's levels connect?
resources.a: A gene mutation changes an enzyme, altering a cell's metabolism and the organism's survival, and the allele's frequency changes over generations

resources.q: All living things are made of one or more cells.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Why is a crystal not alive even though it grows?
resources.a: It has no cells, no genetic material and no metabolism; it grows by adding matter to its surface, not by controlled chemical reactions.

resources.q: Which characteristics of life do viruses lack?
resources.a: Cells and their own metabolism; they can reproduce only inside host cells.

resources.q: Which is a characteristic of all living organisms?
resources.a: They respond to stimuli

resources.q: A new particle found in a hot spring contains RNA and makes copies of itself only inside bacterial cells. How should it be classified?
resources.a: Like a virus: biological but not a living organism by the usual criteria

resources.q: Which pair of observations would most strongly suggest that a sample from Mars was alive?
resources.a: It grows in nutrient medium and passes heritable variation to its offspring

resources.q: Which of these are characteristics shared by all living organisms?
resources.a: Metabolism; Response to stimuli; Reproduction

resources.q: What is an emergent property? Give an example.
resources.a: A property of a whole that its parts lack, for example the heart's pumping, which no single muscle cell can do.

resources.q: What is the difference between a population and a community?
resources.a: A population is one species in an area; a community is all the populations of different species in that area.

resources.q: Which is an organ?
resources.a: The stomach

resources.q: All the trout, algae, insects and plants in a lake, but not the water or rocks, make up a…
resources.a: community

resources.q: Why can't the behaviour of an ecosystem be predicted just by studying each species separately?
resources.a: Interactions between species and with the environment create emergent properties such as nutrient cycling and food-web stability

resources.q: Put these levels in order from smallest to largest.
Why is a prion not considered alive?
resources.a: It is a misfolded protein with no genetic material, no cells and no metabolism of its own.

resources.q: Name three practical ways to test whether a sample contains living cells.
resources.a: Look for growth or reproduction, measure metabolism (for example gas exchange or ATP), and detect DNA or RNA.

resources.q: A seed has been stored dry for 20 years and shows no growth. What is the best description?
resources.a: It is alive but dormant

resources.q: A sample releases CO₂ when given nutrients, but also does so after being heated to 200 °C for an hour. What does this suggest?
resources.a: The CO₂ may come from non-living chemistry, since heating should kill living cells

resources.q: Why did the Viking life-detection results remain controversial?
resources.a: Reactive chemicals in Martian soil could produce gas release without life, and other tests found no organic molecules

resources.q: Explain why a single test, such as measuring gas release, is not enough to show that a sample is alive.
List the taxonomic ranks from broadest to narrowest.
resources.a: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

resources.q: Why are scientific names more useful than common names?
resources.a: Each species has one internationally agreed name, whereas common names vary between languages and regions and can refer to different species.

resources.q: Which is the correct way to write the scientific name of the lion?
resources.a: *Panthera leo*

resources.q: Two populations of frogs look identical but don't interbreed in the wild and their hybrids in the laboratory are sterile. Under the biological species concept they are…
resources.a: separate species

resources.q: Birds are now classified within the reptile clade. What is the main reason?
resources.a: DNA and fossil evidence show birds descend from reptilian (dinosaur) ancestors, so a monophyletic reptile group must include them

resources.q: Put the taxonomic ranks in order, broadest first.
Name the three domains of life.
resources.a: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

resources.q: Which molecule did Woese use to define the domains, and why was it suitable?
resources.a: Small-subunit ribosomal RNA: every cell has it, it has the same function everywhere, and it changes slowly enough to compare very distant organisms.

resources.q: Which organism belongs to the domain Eukarya?
resources.a: A mushroom

resources.q: A newly discovered prokaryote from a deep-sea vent has ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan. Which domain is it most likely in?
resources.a: Archaea

resources.q: What does the finding that archaeal RNA polymerase resembles eukaryotic RNA polymerase suggest?
resources.a: Archaea and eukaryotes share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with bacteria

resources.q: Match each feature to its domain.
How do fungi obtain their food?
resources.a: By secreting digestive enzymes onto organic matter and absorbing the products (saprotrophic nutrition), or as parasites or mutualists.

resources.q: Why is "protist" not a natural group?
resources.a: It includes eukaryotes that are more closely related to animals, plants or fungi than to each other, so it doesn't contain one ancestor and all its descendants.

resources.q: Which feature is shared by fungi and animals but not plants?
resources.a: They are heterotrophic

resources.q: A single-celled eukaryote lives in pond water, has chloroplasts and a flagellum, and can also engulf food in the dark. How is it classified?
resources.a: As a protist

resources.q: DNA studies show fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. Which observation fits this?
resources.a: Fungi and animals both store glycogen and have chitin-related biochemistry, and both are heterotrophs

resources.q: Match each kingdom to its cell-wall material.
What makes a hypothesis scientific?
resources.a: It is testable and falsifiable: some possible result would show it to be wrong.

resources.q: How is a scientific theory different from a hypothesis?
resources.a: A theory is a broad explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence; a hypothesis is a single testable proposal.

resources.q: In science, a theory is…
resources.a: a well-supported explanation based on a large body of evidence

resources.q: Which hypothesis is falsifiable?
resources.a: Plants grown in red light grow taller than plants grown in blue light

resources.q: In Pasteur's experiment, what was the purpose of breaking the neck of a flask after the broth had stayed clear?
resources.a: To show that the broth could still support microbial growth once dust could enter, ruling out the idea that boiling had destroyed its "vital" capacity

resources.q: Put the stages of a scientific investigation in order.
What is a null hypothesis?
resources.a: A statement that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables; statistical tests assess whether the data allow it to be rejected.

resources.q: How is a prediction different from a hypothesis?
resources.a: A hypothesis explains why something happens; a prediction states the specific result expected in a particular test if the hypothesis is correct.

resources.q: Which is a null hypothesis?
resources.a: There is no difference in growth between plants given fertiliser and plants without it

resources.q: A student's hypothesis is that caffeine increases heart rate in water fleas. Which prediction follows from it?
resources.a: Water fleas in caffeine solution will have a higher heart rate than those in pond water alone

resources.q: A test gives p = 0.30 for the difference between two groups. What is the correct conclusion?
resources.a: There is not enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis; the difference could be due to chance

resources.q: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true.
resources.a: False

resources.q: What is a confounding variable?
resources.a: A factor that changes along with the independent variable and could be the real cause of the change in the dependent variable.

resources.q: Why are replicates used?
resources.a: To estimate the variation in results, identify anomalies and give a more reliable mean.

resources.q: In an investigation of how pH affects the rate of an enzyme reaction, the dependent variable is…
resources.a: the rate of the reaction

resources.q: Students find that plants nearer the window grew taller than plants at the back of the room, and conclude that light causes growth. What is the main weakness?
resources.a: Temperature and air flow may also differ near the window, so they are possible confounding variables

resources.q: Why is it better to randomise which seedlings go into each treatment group?
resources.a: So that unknown differences between seedlings are spread evenly and don't bias the comparison

resources.q: Match each variable to its role in an investigation of light intensity and stomatal opening.
A student wants to test whether a new fertiliser increases the yield of tomato plants. Describe a fair experimental design.
What is the purpose of a positive control?
resources.a: To show that the method can detect an effect when one is present, so a negative result isn't just a failure of the method.

resources.q: What is the difference between repeatable and reproducible?
resources.a: Repeatable: the same person gets similar results with the same method; reproducible: other people, possibly with different methods, get similar results.

resources.q: In an experiment on the effect of amylase on starch, which is the best negative control?
resources.a: Starch solution with boiled amylase

resources.q: A drug trial gives one group the drug and another group an identical-looking sugar pill, and neither patients nor doctors know who gets which. This design is called…
resources.a: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

resources.q: A laboratory reports that a gene knock-out doubles lifespan in mice, but three other laboratories find no effect. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
resources.a: The original result is doubtful until it is reproduced; possible causes include chance, differences in conditions or bias

resources.q: Which practices improve the reproducibility of research?
resources.a: Pre-registering the study plan; Sharing raw data and analysis code; Using adequate sample sizes

resources.q: A balance always reads 0.2 g too high. What type of error is this and how could it be corrected?
resources.a: A systematic error; calibrate (zero) the balance, or subtract 0.2 g from each reading.

resources.q: How does taking more repeats improve a result?
resources.a: It reduces the effect of random errors on the mean and makes anomalies easier to spot; it doesn't remove systematic error.

resources.q: Repeated measurements that are very close together but far from the true value are…
resources.a: precise but not accurate

resources.q: Students always read a measuring cylinder from above the meniscus. What effect does this have?
resources.a: A systematic error that makes all volume readings inaccurate in the same direction

resources.q: Two methods measure glucose in the same sample. Method A gives 5.1, 5.0, 5.2 mmol/L; method B gives 4.4, 5.8, 5.0 mmol/L. The true value is 5.0 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
resources.a: A is more precise, and both have means close to the true value

resources.q: A leaf is measured as 52 mm long using a ruler with 1 mm divisions. Taking the uncertainty as half the resolution, what is the percentage uncertainty?
Give one reason a correlation between two variables might not mean that one causes the other.
resources.a: A third (confounding) variable might cause both, or the association might arise by chance.

resources.q: What makes a measurement valid?
resources.a: It measures the quantity it is meant to measure, without being affected by other factors.

resources.q: Results that are similar each time an experiment is repeated are described as…
resources.a: reliable

resources.q: Counting oxygen bubbles from pondweed is said to be less valid than collecting the gas in a syringe. Why?
resources.a: Bubbles vary in size, so the count doesn't measure the volume of oxygen accurately

resources.q: A study finds that people who drink more coffee have lower rates of a disease. Which additional evidence would most support a causal link?
resources.a: A randomised controlled trial in which assigning people to drink coffee lowers the disease rate, with a plausible biological mechanism

resources.q: A method can be reliable but not valid.
resources.a: True

resources.q: State the formula linking magnification, image size and actual size.
resources.a: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size (in the same units).

resources.q: Why must an eyepiece graticule be recalibrated when the objective is changed?
resources.a: The graticule's scale stays the same size in the eyepiece, so the real distance per division changes with magnification.

resources.q: Which unit is most suitable for the diameter of a red blood cell (about 7–8)?
resources.a: micrometres

resources.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. In a photograph it is 30 mm long. What is the magnification?
Two organelles 50 nm apart appear as one blurred spot under a light microscope at ×1,500. Why?
resources.a: The light microscope's resolution (about 200 nm) is coarser than their separation, so extra magnification can't separate them

resources.q: A cell is 8 mm wide in a drawing and actually 40 µm wide. What is the magnification of the drawing?
How many micrometres are there in a millimetre?
How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
Which prefix means 10⁻⁹?
resources.a: nano

resources.q: A plant releases 12 cm³ of oxygen in 4 minutes. What is the rate in cm³ per second?
A cube-shaped cell has sides of 20 µm. What is its volume in mm³?
resources.a: 8 × 10⁻⁶ mm³

resources.q: Convert 3.5 mm to micrometres.
A leaf has an area of 24 cm². What is this in m²?
Write 0.00045 in standard form.
How many significant figures are in 0.0306?
resources.a: Three (3, 0 and 6).

resources.q: What is 6.2 × 10⁻³ written as an ordinary number?
A virus is 1 × 10⁻⁷ m across and a cell 2 × 10⁻⁵ m. How many times wider is the cell?
A population of bacteria grows from 5 × 10³ to 8 × 10⁶ cells. Approximately how many generations (doublings) is this?
resources.a: about 11

resources.q: Calculate (6 × 10⁵) × (3 × 10²) and give the coefficient A when the answer is in standard form, A × 10⁸.
A human body has about 3.7 × 10¹³ cells and about 3.8 × 10¹³ bacteria. What is the ratio of bacteria to human cells (to 2 significant figures)?
Where should units appear in a results table?
resources.a: In the column headings, after the quantity (for example "Time / s"), not in the body of the table.

resources.q: How do you find the rate at a point on a curved graph?
resources.a: Draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate its gradient.

resources.q: Which variable goes on the x-axis?
resources.a: The independent variable

resources.q: A curve of product mass against time flattens out after 5 minutes. What does this show?
resources.a: The rate has fallen to zero, probably because a reactant has been used up

resources.q: On a graph of oxygen volume against time, the tangent at 30 s passes through (0 s, 4 cm³) and (60 s, 22 cm³). What is the rate at 30 s?
resources.a: 0.30 cm³ s⁻¹

resources.q: Match each data set to the best type of graph.
Which test compares observed and expected frequencies in categories?
resources.a: The chi-squared test.

resources.q: What percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution?
resources.a: About 68%.

resources.q: Which measure of spread is most affected by a single extreme value?
resources.a: The range

resources.q: Which test should be used to compare mean leaf length in two populations of normally distributed data?
resources.a: A t-test

resources.q: Group A has mean 50 and standard deviation 2; group B has mean 52 and standard deviation 10. Both groups have 10 measurements. Which statement is best?
resources.a: B's large spread means the 2-unit difference in means may well be due to chance; a statistical test is needed

resources.q: Find the median of 12, 5, 9, 15, 7, 10.
When would systematic sampling along a transect be better than random sampling?
resources.a: When conditions change across the area (a gradient), for example from a woodland edge into a field or down a rocky shore.

resources.q: State two assumptions of mark–release–recapture.
resources.a: No migration, births or deaths between samples; marks don't affect survival or come off; marked individuals mix randomly with the population.

resources.q: Which method is best for estimating the population of daisies on a school field?
resources.a: Random quadrats

resources.q: A survey of a rocky shore records species every 2 m from the low-tide line to the top of the shore. This is…
resources.a: systematic sampling with a transect

resources.q: In a mark–release–recapture study the marks make beetles more visible to birds. How does this affect the estimate?
resources.a: Fewer marked beetles survive to be recaptured, so R is too small and the population is overestimated

resources.q: 40 snails are marked and released. Later 50 are caught, of which 8 are marked. Estimate the population size.
What are the 3Rs?
resources.a: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement of the use of animals in research.

resources.q: What does informed consent require?
resources.a: That participants understand the purpose, procedures and risks, agree voluntarily, and know they can withdraw at any time.

resources.q: Using cell cultures instead of live animals to test a chemical is an example of…
resources.a: replacement

resources.q: A researcher redesigns a study using a statistical power calculation so that 24 mice are needed instead of 40. Which R does this apply?
resources.a: Reduction

resources.q: A study wants to use blood samples collected years ago for routine tests to research a genetic disease. What is the main ethical issue?
resources.a: Whether the donors consented to this new use of their samples and data, and how their privacy is protected

resources.q: Discuss the ethical arguments for and against using animals in medical research.
State the three principles of cell theory.
resources.a: All organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

resources.q: What is the difference between magnification and resolution?
resources.a: Magnification is how much larger the image is; resolution is the smallest separation at which two points can be seen as separate.

resources.q: Who stated that all cells arise from pre-existing cells?
resources.a: Rudolf Virchow

resources.q: A student says a light microscope at ×2000 should show ribosomes clearly. Why is this wrong?
resources.a: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across, far below the light microscope's resolution of about 0.2 µm

resources.q: Which observation would most directly challenge the third principle of cell theory?
resources.a: A new cell forming from non-living chemicals in a sealed sterile flask

resources.q: A mitochondrion is 2 µm long and appears 40 mm long in an electron micrograph. What is the magnification?
Robert Hooke's cork "cells" were living cells with nuclei.
resources.a: False

resources.q: Name four structures found in all prokaryotic cells.
resources.a: Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA (a chromosome in a nucleoid); almost all also have a cell wall.

resources.q: Why can transcription and translation be coupled in bacteria?
resources.a: There is no nuclear envelope separating DNA from ribosomes, so ribosomes can translate mRNA as it is being transcribed.

resources.q: Which structure is found in prokaryotic cells?
resources.a: 70S ribosomes

resources.q: Antibiotic resistance appears in a different bacterial species living in the same gut. What is the most likely route?
resources.a: A plasmid carrying the resistance gene was transferred between the bacteria

resources.q: Why are prokaryotic cells almost never larger than a few micrometres?
resources.a: Without internal transport systems they depend on diffusion, which is only fast enough when the surface area to volume ratio is large

resources.q: Which are typical of prokaryotic cells?
resources.a: Circular chromosome; Plasmids; Cell wall

resources.q: Give three differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
resources.a: Eukaryotes have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and linear chromosomes with histones (and 80S ribosomes); prokaryotes have a nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles and usually a circular chromosome (70S ribosomes).

resources.q: Give two pieces of evidence that mitochondria were once bacteria.
resources.a: They have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by fission.

resources.q: Which feature is found in eukaryotic but not prokaryotic cells?
resources.a: A nuclear envelope

resources.q: An organism is single-celled, has a nucleus and mitochondria, and no cell wall. What is it?
resources.a: A eukaryote such as an amoeba

resources.q: Why do mitochondria have ribosomes that resemble bacterial ribosomes?
resources.a: They are descended from bacteria and kept part of their own protein-making system

resources.q: Yeast cells are eukaryotic.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
resources.a: A cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts (and usually a large permanent vacuole).

resources.q: Why does a red blood cell burst in pure water?
resources.a: Water enters by osmosis and, with no cell wall to resist expansion, the membrane stretches until it ruptures.

resources.q: Which organelle carries out aerobic respiration in an animal cell?
resources.a: Mitochondrion

resources.q: A cell secretes large amounts of protein hormone. Which pair of organelles would you expect to be especially extensive?
resources.a: Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus

resources.q: White blood cells can engulf bacteria but plant cells cannot. What best explains the difference?
resources.a: Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall, so their membrane can extend around particles

resources.q: Which structure is found in animal cells but not in plant cells?
resources.a: Centrioles in a centrosome

resources.q: Animal cells have centrioles in their centrosome, while most plant cells do not.
resources.a: True

resources.q: What does the tonoplast surround?
resources.a: The large permanent vacuole of a plant cell.

resources.q: Why does a plant wilt when short of water?
resources.a: Its cells lose water, turgor pressure falls, and the cells no longer press against each other to support the stem and leaves.

resources.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
resources.a: Cellulose cell wall

resources.q: A cell from a carrot root has a cell wall and a large vacuole but no chloroplasts. What does this show?
resources.a: It is a plant cell from a non-photosynthetic tissue

resources.q: Why can a cell with a wall withstand being placed in pure water, when an animal cell cannot?
resources.a: The wall resists expansion, so turgor pressure builds up until water stops entering

resources.q: Which three structures do plant cells have that animal cells lack?
resources.a: Cell wall, large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts

resources.q: Match each plant cell structure to its function.
What are fungal cell walls made of?
resources.a: Mainly chitin, with glucans.

resources.q: How does a fungus digest its food?
resources.a: It secretes enzymes into its surroundings to break food down outside its body, then absorbs the products through its hyphae.

resources.q: Which feature distinguishes fungal cells from plant cells?
resources.a: Chitin cell walls

resources.q: Bread mould spreads over a slice of bread and the bread softens beneath it. What explains the softening?
resources.a: Enzymes secreted by the hyphae digest the bread outside the fungus

resources.q: Why does a mycelium suit a fungus's way of feeding?
resources.a: Its branching threads give an enormous surface area for secreting enzymes and absorbing nutrients

resources.q: Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Why do Gram-positive bacteria stain purple?
resources.a: Their thick peptidoglycan layer keeps the crystal violet stain after the decolourising step.

resources.q: Why doesn't penicillin harm human cells?
resources.a: It blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, which human cells don't have.

resources.q: What is the bacterial cell wall made of?
resources.a: Peptidoglycan

resources.q: A bacterium stains pink after a Gram stain. What does this tell you about its structure?
resources.a: It has a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane

resources.q: Penicillin kills actively dividing bacteria but has little effect on bacteria that are not growing. Why?
resources.a: It stops new peptidoglycan cross-links forming, which only matters while cells are building new wall

resources.q: Put the steps of a Gram stain in order.
Which organelles belong to the endomembrane system?
resources.a: The nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vesicles and the plasma membrane.

resources.q: Why are mitochondria not part of the endomembrane system?
resources.a: They are not connected to it by vesicle traffic; they grow and divide on their own and import proteins directly from the cytosol.

resources.q: Which organelle packages proteins into vesicles for secretion?
resources.a: Golgi apparatus

resources.q: A drug stops vesicles from budding off the ER. What happens to a protein destined for secretion?
resources.a: It builds up in the ER and is not secreted

resources.q: Cells lining the stomach secrete a lot of enzyme and also divide often. Which combination of organelles would you expect to be prominent?
resources.a: Extensive rough ER and Golgi, many mitochondria, and active nuclei with large nucleoli

resources.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
resources.a: The mitochondrion

resources.q: Put the stages of making and secreting a protein in order.
What passes out of the nucleus through the nuclear pores?
resources.a: mRNA and ribosomal subunits (and other RNAs); proteins such as histones and transcription factors pass in.

resources.q: What is made in the nucleolus?
resources.a: Ribosomal RNA, which is combined with proteins to form ribosomal subunits.

resources.q: What are histones?
resources.a: Proteins around which DNA is wound in chromatin

resources.q: A cell is treated with a chemical that blocks nuclear pores. Which process stops first?
resources.a: Export of mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm

resources.q: Why does a mature mammalian red blood cell have a limited lifespan of about 120 days?
resources.a: It has no nucleus, so it can't make new proteins to repair itself or divide

resources.q: What is made in the nucleolus?
resources.a: Ribosomal RNA and ribosome subunits

resources.q: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Where in the mitochondrion does the Krebs cycle take place?
resources.a: In the matrix.

resources.q: Why do mitochondria have folded inner membranes?
resources.a: The cristae increase the surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so more ATP can be made.

resources.q: Which part of a mitochondrion contains ATP synthase?
resources.a: The inner membrane

resources.q: Sperm cells have many mitochondria packed around the base of the tail. What does this suggest?
resources.a: Swimming uses a lot of ATP, supplied close to where it is needed

resources.q: A poison blocks the electron transport chain. Why does ATP production fall sharply even though glycolysis can continue?
resources.a: Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation, which depends on the electron transport chain building the proton gradient

resources.q: Why do muscle cells contain many mitochondria?
resources.a: They need a lot of ATP from aerobic respiration

resources.q: Mitochondrial DNA is usually inherited from the father.
resources.a: False

resources.q: Where in the chloroplast is chlorophyll found?
resources.a: In the thylakoid membranes.

resources.q: What is fixed in the Calvin cycle, and where does it happen?
resources.a: Carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar, in the stroma.

resources.q: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
resources.a: On the thylakoid membranes

resources.q: Palisade cells have far more chloroplasts than spongy mesophyll cells. Why?
resources.a: They are nearest the upper surface and receive the most light

resources.q: A plant is kept in light but with no carbon dioxide. Which process stops, and why?
resources.a: The Calvin cycle, because it needs carbon dioxide to fix into sugar

resources.q: In which part of a chloroplast are the light-dependent reactions?
resources.a: The thylakoid membranes

resources.q: Which features do chloroplasts share with bacteria?
resources.a: Circular DNA; 70S ribosomes; Division by fission

resources.q: Where are proteins for secretion made?
resources.a: On ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

resources.q: Why don't a ribosome's subunit S values add up (50S + 30S = 70S)?
resources.a: Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on shape as well as mass, so they are not additive.

resources.q: What are ribosomes made of?
resources.a: Ribosomal RNA and proteins

resources.q: Tetracycline binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Why does it harm bacteria more than human cells?
resources.a: Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, with a 40S small subunit that it binds poorly

resources.q: Some antibiotics that act on bacterial ribosomes cause side effects in tissues with high energy demand. What is a likely explanation?
resources.a: Mitochondria have bacterial-type ribosomes, so the drug can reduce mitochondrial protein synthesis

resources.q: What does a tRNA molecule carry to the ribosome?
resources.a: A specific amino acid, matched by its anticodon

resources.q: Ribosomes are surrounded by a single membrane.
resources.a: False

resources.q: Name three functions of smooth ER.
resources.a: Making lipids (phospholipids, cholesterol, steroid hormones), detoxifying drugs and storing calcium ions.

resources.q: What happens to proteins inside the rough ER?
resources.a: They fold with the help of chaperones and are modified, for example by glycosylation; misfolded proteins are held back and destroyed.

resources.q: Which cell would have the most smooth ER?
resources.a: A cell of the adrenal cortex making steroid hormones

resources.q: Regular heavy drinking increases the amount of smooth ER in liver cells. Why?
resources.a: The liver cells detoxify more alcohol and make more of the enzymes, and membrane, to do it

resources.q: A mutation causes a secreted protein to fold incorrectly. Where is the protein most likely to be found, and why?
resources.a: Retained in the ER and broken down, because ER quality control stops misfolded proteins moving on

resources.q: Match each cell to the type of ER it has most of.
What are the cis and trans faces of the Golgi?
resources.a: The cis face receives vesicles from the ER; the trans face sends vesicles on to their destinations.

resources.q: How are enzymes directed to lysosomes?
resources.a: They are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi, and receptors for this tag send them to lysosomes.

resources.q: What is the main function of the Golgi apparatus?
resources.a: Modifying, sorting and packaging proteins and lipids

resources.q: Radioactive amino acids are given to a pancreatic cell. In which order would the label appear?
resources.a: Rough ER, then Golgi, then secretory vesicles

resources.q: In I-cell disease, lysosomal enzymes are found in the blood, while patients' lysosomes fill with undigested material. What is the underlying fault?
resources.a: The enzymes are not tagged with mannose-6-phosphate, so they are secreted instead of sent to lysosomes

resources.q: What does the Golgi apparatus do?
resources.a: Modifies, packages and sends proteins to their destinations

resources.q: Proteins move through the Golgi from the cis face to the trans face.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Why is the inside of a lysosome kept acidic?
resources.a: Its hydrolytic enzymes work best at about pH 4.5–5, and the acidity keeps them active inside while making them less harmful if they leak.

resources.q: What does catalase do?
resources.a: It breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

resources.q: What is autophagy?
resources.a: Lysosomes digesting the cell's own worn-out organelles

resources.q: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium. Which organelle fuses with the vesicle containing it?
resources.a: A lysosome

resources.q: Why might a small leak from a lysosome do little harm to the cell?
resources.a: Lysosomal enzymes work poorly at the neutral pH of the cytosol

resources.q: Tay–Sachs disease is caused by a missing lysosomal enzyme.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Which cytoskeletal filament forms the spindle in cell division?
resources.a: Microtubules.

resources.q: What do kinesin and dynein do?
resources.a: They are motor proteins that move cargo such as vesicles along microtubules, using ATP.

resources.q: Which protein makes up microtubules?
resources.a: Tubulin

resources.q: People with primary ciliary dyskinesia have faulty dynein arms in their cilia. Which problem would you expect?
resources.a: Repeated chest infections, because airway cilia can't clear mucus

resources.q: Colchicine stops microtubules from forming. Why does it block cell division?
resources.a: The spindle that separates chromosomes is made of microtubules

resources.q: Match each filament to a role.
What does partially permeable mean?
resources.a: Letting some substances pass through but not others.

resources.q: Name three functions of the plasma membrane besides controlling what passes.
resources.a: Cell signalling (receptors), cell recognition (glycoproteins), and attachment to other cells or the matrix.

resources.q: Which substance crosses a phospholipid bilayer most easily without a protein?
resources.a: Oxygen

resources.q: Why can a mitochondrion make ATP only when its inner membrane is intact?
resources.a: ATP synthesis depends on a proton gradient that only an intact membrane can maintain

resources.q: A cell is placed in a solution containing a dye that can't cross membranes. The dye stays outside but the cell keeps importing glucose. What does this show about the membrane?
resources.a: It is selectively permeable, with transport proteins for some substances but not others

resources.q: Which are functions of membrane proteins?
resources.a: Transport; Receiving signals; Catalysing reactions

resources.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer in water?
resources.a: Their hydrophobic tails avoid water by facing each other in the middle, while their hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides.

resources.q: What does cholesterol do in animal membranes?
resources.a: It regulates fluidity: it reduces fluidity and permeability at body temperature and prevents tight packing when cold.

resources.q: Which part of a phospholipid is hydrophobic?
resources.a: The fatty acid tails

resources.q: In a famous experiment, a mouse cell and a human cell were fused, with their membrane proteins labelled in different colours. Within 40 minutes the colours were mixed over the whole surface. What does this show?
resources.a: Membrane proteins move sideways within a fluid bilayer

resources.q: Bacteria grown at low temperature make membranes with more unsaturated fatty acids. Why does this help?
resources.a: Kinked unsaturated tails pack less tightly, keeping the membrane fluid enough to work in the cold

resources.q: In the fluid mosaic model, carbohydrate chains are found mainly on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
resources.a: True

resources.q: Which transport processes are passive?
resources.a: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis.

resources.q: Why can't ions diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer?
resources.a: They are charged and surrounded by a shell of water, so they can't dissolve in the hydrophobic core.

resources.q: Which process needs ATP?
resources.a: Active transport

resources.q: A substance moves into a cell against its concentration gradient, and the movement stops when a respiratory poison is added. What is the mechanism?
resources.a: Active transport

resources.q: Steroid hormones such as testosterone act on receptors inside cells, while insulin acts on receptors in the plasma membrane. What explains the difference?
resources.a: Steroids are small and lipid-soluble so they cross the bilayer; insulin is a large polar protein that can't

resources.q: Match each substance to how it most likely crosses the plasma membrane.
State Fick's law.
resources.a: Rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area × concentration difference ÷ thickness of the exchange surface.

resources.q: Why is diffusion faster at higher temperature?
resources.a: Particles have more kinetic energy and move faster.

resources.q: Which change would speed up diffusion of oxygen into the blood?
resources.a: A thinner barrier between air and blood

resources.q: In emphysema, alveolar walls break down into fewer, larger air spaces. Why does this make people breathless?
resources.a: The surface area for gas exchange falls, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood

resources.q: Why are single-celled organisms able to rely on diffusion while a mouse cannot?
resources.a: A small organism has a large surface area to volume ratio and short diffusion distances

resources.q: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 10 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio (as x : 1)?
What is the water potential of pure water?
resources.a: Zero (0 kPa).

resources.q: What happens to a red blood cell in distilled water, and why?
resources.a: Water enters by osmosis because the cell has a lower water potential; with no wall, the cell swells and bursts (haemolysis).

resources.q: Which solution has the highest water potential?
resources.a: Pure water

resources.q: Potato cylinders are left in a range of sucrose solutions. In which solution would they gain mass?
resources.a: One with a higher water potential than the potato cells

resources.q: Intravenous drips use saline of about 0.9% sodium chloride rather than pure water. Why?
resources.a: It has about the same water potential as blood plasma, so red blood cells neither swell nor shrink

resources.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −850 kPa and a pressure potential of +350 kPa. What is its water potential, in kPa?
A plant cell placed in a concentrated salt solution can become plasmolysed.
resources.a: True

resources.q: How do carrier proteins move molecules across a membrane?
resources.a: They bind a specific molecule, change shape and release it on the other side.

resources.q: Why does the rate of facilitated diffusion level off at high concentration?
resources.a: All the transport proteins are occupied, so adding more substance can't increase the rate.

resources.q: Which statement about facilitated diffusion is correct?
resources.a: It moves substances down their concentration gradient through specific proteins

resources.q: A graph of uptake rate against external glucose concentration rises and then levels off. What does this suggest?
resources.a: Glucose enters by facilitated diffusion through a limited number of carriers

resources.q: After a meal, insulin speeds glucose uptake into muscle cells even though the glucose gradient hardly changes. How?
resources.a: It causes more GLUT4 carriers to be inserted into the membrane, increasing the maximum rate

resources.q: Channel proteins can be specific for particular ions.
resources.a: True

resources.q: How many sodium and potassium ions does the sodium–potassium pump move per ATP?
resources.a: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

resources.q: Why is glucose absorption in the intestine called secondary active transport?
resources.a: The co-transporter uses the sodium gradient, which is made by the ATP-driven Na⁺/K⁺ pump, rather than ATP directly.

resources.q: What does the sodium–potassium pump use as its energy source?
resources.a: ATP

resources.q: Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from soil where nitrate is less concentrated than inside the cells. Which feature would you expect these cells to have?
resources.a: Many mitochondria to supply ATP for active transport

resources.q: Ouabain blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Why does it also stop glucose absorption by intestinal cells?
resources.a: Without the pump, the sodium gradient that drives the glucose co-transporter runs down

resources.q: Put the steps of active transport by a carrier protein in order.
What is the difference between phagocytosis and pinocytosis?
resources.a: Phagocytosis takes in large solid particles; pinocytosis takes in droplets of fluid.

resources.q: Give two examples of exocytosis.
resources.a: Secretion of digestive enzymes or insulin, and release of neurotransmitter at a synapse.

resources.q: Which process releases neurotransmitter at a synapse?
resources.a: Exocytosis

resources.q: A macrophage engulfs a bacterium. Which organelle will the resulting vesicle fuse with?
resources.a: A lysosome

resources.q: People with familial hypercholesterolaemia have high blood cholesterol even on a low-fat diet. Using what you know about transport, explain why.
resources.a: Faulty LDL receptors stop receptor-mediated endocytosis of cholesterol, so it stays in the blood

resources.q: Exocytosis adds membrane to the cell surface.
resources.a: True

resources.q: How is a red blood cell adapted for carrying oxygen?
resources.a: Biconcave shape for a large surface area and flexibility; no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

resources.q: Why do root hair cells have long projections?

resources.q: Which feature of a sperm cell helps it penetrate the egg?

resources.q: Cells lining the small intestine have microvilli and many mitochondria. What do these suggest about their function?
resources.a: They absorb nutrients, partly by active transport

resources.a: Most mature neurons can't divide and the brain has few stem cells to replace them, while skin has active stem cells

resources.a: Self-renewal (dividing to make more stem cells) and differentiation into specialised cells.

resources.q: Why does a bone marrow transplant restore all types of blood cell?
resources.a: It provides multipotent haematopoietic stem cells, which make every kind of blood cell

resources.q: What is the main advantage of iPSCs over embryonic stem cells for treating a patient?
resources.a: They can be made from the patient's own cells, avoiding rejection and the destruction of embryos

resources.q: Most adult stem cells are pluripotent.

resources.q: What do transcription factors do?

resources.q: What causes cells to differentiate?
resources.a: Differences in which genes are expressed

resources.a: The specialised nucleus still contains all the genes needed to make a whole organism

resources.q: Why do steroid hormones have intracellular receptors?

resources.q: Which type of signalling uses hormones carried in the blood?

resources.q: Adrenaline makes liver cells release glucose but has no effect on many other cells. Why?

resources.q: One molecule of adrenaline can lead to the release of millions of glucose molecules. What explains this?
resources.a: Each step of the second-messenger cascade activates many molecules of the next

resources.q: Put the steps of adrenaline signalling in a liver cell in order.
Which junction lets heart muscle cells contract together?

resources.q: What do tight junctions do in the lining of the small intestine?

resources.q: Which junction links the cytoplasm of neighbouring animal cells?
resources.a: Gap junction

resources.q: In pemphigus, antibodies attack desmosome proteins in the skin. What would you expect?
resources.a: Blisters, as layers of skin cells separate

resources.q: Why does the blood–brain barrier depend especially on tight junctions?
resources.a: They stop substances passing between the cells of capillary walls, so entry is controlled by the cells' transporters

resources.q: Match each junction to its function.
Name the four main types of animal tissue.
resources.a: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue.

resources.q: Why does the stomach count as an organ?
resources.a: It is made of several tissues (epithelium, muscle, connective and nervous tissue) working together to digest food.

resources.q: Which is a tissue?

resources.q: Xylem, phloem and mesophyll are found together in a leaf. What is the leaf?
resources.a: An organ, made of several tissues

resources.q: Why can't a large animal rely on diffusion across its skin for its oxygen supply, as a flatworm can?
resources.a: Its surface area to volume ratio is small and most cells are far from the surface, so it needs lungs and a circulation

resources.q: Put these in order from smallest to largest level of organisation.
Which four elements make up about 96% of living mass?
resources.a: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.

resources.q: What is released when a condensation reaction joins two monomers?
resources.a: A molecule of water.

resources.q: Which element can form four covalent bonds and so build the skeletons of biological molecules?
resources.a: Carbon

resources.q: What happens in a hydrolysis reaction?
resources.a: A bond is broken by adding a water molecule

resources.q: Why are weak interactions such as hydrogen bonds important in large biological molecules?
resources.a: Many of them together stabilise shape while still allowing changes needed for function

Why is water a good solvent for ions?
resources.a: Its polar molecules surround and separate charged particles.

resources.q: Why does sweating cool the body?
resources.a: Evaporation of water absorbs a large amount of heat energy (high latent heat of vaporisation).

resources.q: Why is water described as polar?
resources.a: Oxygen pulls electrons more strongly, giving partial charges

resources.q: Which property helps keep lake temperatures stable through the day?
resources.a: High specific heat capacity

resources.q: Why does ice floating benefit aquatic life in winter?
resources.a: It forms an insulating layer so water below stays liquid

resources.q: Match each property to an example.

resources.a: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds rather than two

resources.a: Strands can be separated for replication and transcription

What is the normal pH range of human blood?

resources.a: HCO₃⁻ combines with H⁺ to form H₂CO₃

resources.q: Why do triglycerides store more energy per gram than carbohydrates?

resources.a: They contact the hydrophobic interior of the lipid bilayer

How many subunits does haemoglobin have?

resources.a: A non-protein part permanently attached to a protein, such as haem.

resources.a: Hydrophobic interactions burying non-polar groups

resources.a: Albumin is irreversibly denatured and aggregated

resources.a: Exons

resources.a: The addition of carbohydrate groups to a protein

resources.a: They express different sets of genes

resources.a: Their receptors act as transcription factors

resources.a: The silencing of one X chromosome in each cell of female mammals.

resources.a: Heritable changes in gene expression without DNA sequence changes

resources.a: Nonsense

resources.a: When it is not repaired before replication copies the error.

resources.a: Reactive oxygen species from respiration

resources.a: They can cause loss or rearrangement of chromosome sections

resources.a: Many mutagens detected in bacteria are also carcinogens in humans

resources.q: Which master transcription factor drives muscle identity?
